about.label: About the project
about.statement: Our aim is to supply quality bromine to Indian industry and reduce its dependence on imports.
about.body: Hari Hara Serenity Chemical LLP is setting up a plant at Rapar, Kachchh, Gujarat, to recover and purify bromine from bittern, the residual brine left after salt production. Bromine is a key input for the pharmaceutical, agrochemical, flame-retardant, water-treatment and oil-field chemical industries.
about.photo_alt: Landscape view of coastal salt flats
about.why_p1: Indian industry depends on imports for bromine. Our aim is to reduce that dependence by producing bromine at home.
about.why_p2: Salt production along Gujarat's coast leaves behind bittern, a mineral-rich residual brine. Recovering bromine from it makes further use of a material the salt industry already produces.
about.why_p3: The plant is still under development. This website describes what we are working towards.

blocks.title: A rare liquid element
blocks.text: Bromine is a dense, reddish-brown liquid with a sharp smell. Along with mercury, it is one of only two elements that are liquid at normal room temperature.

blocks.title: Where it comes from
blocks.text: Bromine occurs as bromide, a compound dissolved in seawater, salt lakes and natural brines. When seawater is evaporated to make salt, the bromide stays behind and becomes concentrated in the leftover brine, called bittern.

blocks.title: A discovery from salt brine
blocks.text: Bromine was first isolated in the 1820s by the French chemist Antoine-Jerome Balard, who found it in the residue of salt-marsh brine near Montpellier.

blocks.title: How it got its name
blocks.text: The name comes from the Greek word bromos, meaning stench, because of its strong smell.

blocks.title: Handled with care
blocks.text: Bromine is toxic and corrosive. This is why its production and handling are regulated, and why any plant that works with it must meet strict safety and environmental requirements.
